reconcile.connective: Defenders read the two totals as different slices of one administrative pyramid — Gill counts the top tier of 250 together with the 300 above the 3,300 to reach the 550.

discrepancy.connective: A harmonizing commentary itself concedes the figures cannot simply be added or distinguished — the underlying text is corrupt in one of the two books.

excerpts.excerpt_text: It is generally agreed that the text of one of these passages is corrupt.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB, a harmonizing commentary, concedes that the 250/550 divergence is a genuine textual corruption rather than two reconcilable counts — a verbatim discrepancy-direction concession from a gathered note (spec line 81-84).

excerpts.excerpt_text: in Ch2 8:10 they are said to be but two hundred and fifty; now it may be observed, as is by the Jewish writers, that there were three sorts of those rulers; the lowest rank and order of them consisted of 3300, the next of three hundred which were over the 3300, and being numbered with them made 3600, Ch2 2:18 and the highest rank of them were two hundred and fifty, and the middlemost and highest being joined together, as they are here, made five hundred and fifty.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill directly addresses 550 vs 250: a three-tier scheme where the top rank of 250 joined to the 300 middle rank yields the 550 of Kings, so the numbers describe overlapping groups, not a contradiction.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on 1 Kings 9:23
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, offering two harmonizations of 550 vs 250: the rabbinic three-tier count (250 + 300 = 550) and Abarbanel's distinction between overseers of temple work and overseers throughout the kingdom.
